passages.heading: Restaurant Technology Platform
passages.text: Fast-tracked product–market fit for front and back of house technology in the restaurant industry. Three systems, built in the order that let each one pay for the next.

passages.heading: Restaurant Technology Platform
passages.text: Front of house came first: point-of-sale, kitchen display system, loyalty programme and real-time analytics. Getting the transaction layer right early meant every later system had trustworthy data to read from, rather than a reporting pipeline bolted on after the fact.

passages.heading: Restaurant Technology Platform
passages.text: The IoT layer was built with Operations rather than for them, because the waste it targeted was operational, not technical. An ESP32-based system handled temperature monitoring, energy metering and AI-on-the-edge detection, with EMQX as the broker. Inference runs on the device: a kitchen with intermittent connectivity still needs its cold storage watched, and paying to stream raw sensor data to the cloud to answer a question the device can answer itself is a cost with no matching benefit.

passages.heading: Restaurant Technology Platform
passages.text: Menu planning was the piece that needed AI to be worth anything. It uses an LLM with vector search to query product mix data and infer location-specific variations — the same dish sells differently two kilometres apart, and the interesting signal is in that variation rather than in the aggregate. Retrieval over real product mix data, not a model asked to guess at a menu.

passages.heading: Restaurant Technology Platform
passages.text: I also took ownership of product management directly, driving the roadmap for B2B value-added services and loyalty features.

passages.heading: Restaurant Technology Platform
passages.text: From MVP to 100+ outlets in 6 months. Increased RPR

passages.heading: Ghost Kitchen Startup
passages.text: The platform worked but the unit economics did not scale: cost per outlet was not falling as outlets were added. Refactoring the entire technology platform was the only way to change that shape, so it was a cost-structure problem before it was an engineering one.

passages.heading: Ghost Kitchen Startup
passages.text: Migrating AWS to GCP and repurchasing cloud-native ERP. Repurchasing rather than migrating the existing ERP was the harder call and the right one — carrying a self-managed system into a new environment would have moved the licence and operational burden intact rather than removing it.

passages.heading: Ghost Kitchen Startup
passages.text: Then developer experience, treated as a cost lever rather than a perk. GitHub Actions, Terraform and Go, leaning on managed GCP services wherever running something ourselves earned nothing. Release cycle time is the metric that compounds: everything downstream of it gets cheaper when it drops.

passages.heading: Ghost Kitchen Startup
passages.text: And the org chart, because the expense line is mostly people. Trainee and upskilling programmes to build capability in-house, with outsourcing reserved for genuinely specialised work. Buying permanent headcount for a temporary specialism is how technology budgets quietly ratchet upward.

passages.heading: Ghost Kitchen Startup
passages.text: 80% reduction in ICT-related expenses. 50% faster release cycle

passages.heading: Multinational Retail Company
passages.text: A B2B2C e-commerce transformation three years behind schedule, and a USD 3 million ERP and WMS migration that was not going to land. The first job was triage.

passages.heading: Multinational Retail Company
passages.text: The rescue turned on scope, not delivery speed. The programme was replacing ERP and WMS together. I implemented the new WMS and kept the legacy ERP for financials and manufacturing — the warehouse was where the pain and the return actually were, and the financial modules were working. That split is what realised the ROI on a project already written off, and it is the decision I would point to first: the fastest way to finish was to stop doing part of it.

passages.heading: Multinational Retail Company
passages.text: The transformation then completed in nine months after three years of not completing, on an IT function re-engineered to deliver rather than a longer timeline.

passages.heading: Multinational Retail Company
passages.text: From there the work was compounding rather than corrective: refactoring the distributor point-of-sale system; seamless omnichannel UX across e-commerce, point-of-sale and loyalty, which is what moved customer lifetime value; and consolidating disparate sales, stock and assortment data into PowerBI dashboards to give a distributor 360 view — the reporting nobody could assemble while the data sat in separate systems.

passages.heading: Multinational Retail Company
passages.text: Finally, harmonising IT systems across affiliates in Vietnam, Malaysia and the Philippines with a global cross-functional team, so regional expansion had something to expand onto. Social commerce across Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines scaled to 1.5 million monthly active users.

passages.heading: Multinational Retail Company

passages.heading: Browser-Local Semantic Search
passages.text: The Ask page on this site answers questions about these case studies by running a sentence embedding model inside the visitor's browser. There is no inference server, no API key and no request carrying the question anywhere. It is small, and it is deliberately small: the point was to build the thing end to end rather than describe having once specified it.

passages.heading: Browser-Local Semantic Search
passages.text: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, quantised to 8-bit, executed by ONNX Runtime on WebAssembly through Transformers.js. Quantisation is what makes the model shippable at all — full precision is four times the weight for a retrieval quality difference this corpus cannot resolve. The runtime runs single-threaded because GitHub Pages cannot send the COOP and COEP headers that SharedArrayBuffer requires, so the threaded build would silently fall back anyway. I measured crossOriginIsolated in the deployed page rather than assuming it.

passages.heading: Browser-Local Semantic Search
passages.text: The model, the runtime and the weights are all served from this origin. The obvious build fetches them from a model hub on first use. That would mean pinning a CDN script by SRI digest in one breath and then pulling tens of megabytes of unpinned executable WebAssembly from a third party in the next — the same integrity problem an order of magnitude larger. Vendoring costs repository size and buys a page with no third-party requests at all, which I verified in the network panel rather than in the source.

passages.heading: Browser-Local Semantic Search
passages.text: Retrieval is an exhaustive cosine scan, not an approximate index. A few dozen passages at 384 dimensions is under ten thousand multiply-accumulates — microseconds, and four orders of magnitude below the cost of embedding the question that precedes it. An HNSW graph would add a dependency, a build artefact and a recall tradeoff to optimise the part that is already free. Knowing where that crossover sits is the engineering; reaching for the vector database before it is the failure mode.

passages.heading: Browser-Local Semantic Search
passages.text: The corpus is parsed out of this page at load time rather than committed as a generated embeddings file, so there is no build step to forget and no way for the index to describe a version of these case studies that no longer exists.

passages.heading: Browser-Local Semantic Search
passages.text: No inference cost and no data egress — the question never leaves the tab. ~25ms per query after a one-time model load. Zero third-party requests at runtime
